title: Cyclone Murasu races across Bay of Bengal, IMD warns of storm surges up to 1.5 metres
content: Cyclone Murasu moved across the Bay of Bengal at speeds reaching 27km/h. The severe cyclonic storm is expected to make landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast early on November 3. Storm surges of 1–1.5 metres could flood low-lying coastal areas. Seawater could reach up to 330 metres inland in Ongole and 190 metres in Bapatla. Severe cyclone Murasu is hurtling rapidly towards the Andhra Pradesh coast, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) warning that storm surges of up to 1.5 metres could inundate low-lying coastal areas during landfall on the night of November 2-3. The storm comes just days after the very severe cyclonic storm Arnab made landfall further north along the same coastline on October 28, 2026. Murasu is expected to make landfall south of Ongole, between Nellore and Narsapur, between 11:30 pm on November 2 and 4 am on November 3, bringing strong winds, storm surges and possible coastal flooding. What sets Cyclone Murasu apart is the speed at which it has travelled across the Bay of Bengal. However, the storm slowed to 10 km/h during the six hours preceding 2:30 pm on November 2, according to the latest IMD update. Rapidly moving cyclones generally have less time to intensify before reaching land. The IMD forecasts that Murasu will make landfall as a severe cyclonic storm, with sustained wind speeds of 100–110 km/h and gusts reaching 120 km/h. The cyclone is being continuously monitored by Doppler weather radars in Chennai, Machilipatnam and Visakhapatnam.

content: A new study reveals that the amount of carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism has increased dramatically over three decades. The carbon dioxide produced by human bodies as they convert food into energy increased by 74% over three decades, according to a University of Bath-led study. By 2015, the global total had reached an estimated 2.05 billion metric tons (2.26 billion U.S. tons) annually, highlighting a substantial component of the Earth’s carbon cycle that scientists had not previously quantified on this scale. Unlike emissions from burning fossil fuels, the CO 2 humans exhale largely comes from carbon recently absorbed from the atmosphere by plants and transferred through food. Burning coal, oil, and natural gas releases carbon that has been stored underground for millions of years, adding it to the active carbon cycle. Published in The Lancet Planetary Health , the study found that annual CO 2 production from human metabolism rose from 1.18 billion metric tons (1.30 billion U.S. tons) in 1985 to 2.05 billion metric tons (2.26 billion U.S. tons) in 2015. More than 60% of that increase was attributable to population growth rather than a substantial rise in the amount produced by each individual. To estimate global emissions from metabolism, the researchers analyzed thousands of real-world measurements of CO 2 production in people ranging from infants to older adults. They combined these findings with worldwide population and body weight data to calculate how human metabolic activity changed over time. Professor Javier Gonzalez, who led the research at the University of Bath’s Centre for Exercise, Nutrition and Metabolism, explained: “We all produce carbon dioxide simply by turning food into energy, but until now we haven’t had a good idea how much that adds up to worldwide. “What we’ve found is that the increase is mainly because there are more of us. This gives scientists one more piece of the puzzle when working out where carbon comes from and where it goes. Ultimately, this information can help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be.” Human metabolism contributes to the continuous movement of carbon through the environment, particularly in densely populated cities. Accounting for that activity could help researchers develop more accurate carbon budgets and better assess the effects of strategies designed to reduce emissions. The researchers emphasize that their findings do not suggest people should exercise less, change their diets, or attempt to reduce the carbon dioxide they breathe out. The purpose is to improve scientific measurements of carbon movement, not identify respiration as a contributor to fossil fuel emissions. Gonzalez stressed the distinction: “The important thing is that the carbon dioxide we breathe out is not the same as burning fossil fuels. We’re not saying that breathing is driving climate change. “What this study does is give us a much clearer picture of how much CO 2 people produce around the world, and how that is changing as the population grows. This understanding can help improve the accuracy predictions of carbon reduction programs.” Reference: “Accounting for global carbon dioxide production from human metabolism between 1985 and 2015: a modelling study” by Javier T Gonzalez, Lorenzo Lolli, Bruno Spellanzon, Greg Atkinson, Ed Maunder, Alfonso Moreno-Cabañas, Jariya Buniam, Dylan Thompson, James Betts, Philip N Ainslie, Heliodoro Alemán-Mateo, Linda Bandini, Ellen E Blaak, Carlijn V C Bouten, Pascal Bovet, Soren Brage, Regina Casper, Prasangi Dabare, Barry W Fudge, Melanie Gillingham, Annalies H Goris, Michael Gurven, Hinke Haisma, Marije B Hoos, Noorjehan Joonas, Peter Katzmarzyk, Misaka Kimura, Sai Krupa Das, Pulani Lanerolle, Christel L Larsson, Marie Löf, Aviva Must, Marian Neuhouser, Theresa A Nicklas, Robert M Ojiambo, Kirsi H Pietilainen, Susan B Racette, Eric Ravussin, Leanne M Redman, John J Reilly, Susan Roberts, Luis B Sardinha, Analiza M Silva, Srishti Sinha, Anders M Sjödin, Eric Stice, Samuel S Urlacher, Edgar A Van Mil, Jeanine A Verbunt, Jonathan C K Wells, Tsukasa Yoshida, Xueying Zhang, Alexia Murphy-Alford, Cornelia U Loechl, Amy Luke, Michele Novaes Ravelli, Herman Pontzer, Jennifer Rood, Hiroyuki Sagayama, Dale A Schoeller, Klaas R Westerterp, William W Wong, Yosuke Yamada and John Speakman, 26 October 2026, The Lancet Planetary Health .
